identity.title: Interpreting Emergent Planning in Model-Free Reinforcement Learning

problem.claim: The paper asks whether model-free reinforcement learning agents can learn to plan, and how such planning is internally represented and affects behavior.

gap.claim: The authors state that mechanistic evidence for planning learned by model-free reinforcement learning agents was previously lacking.

contributions.claim: Applies concept-based interpretability to a model-free agent playing Sokoban, probing planning-relevant concepts, examining plan formation, and using interventions to test behavioral influence.
Reports that DRC uses learned concept representations to formulate plans that predict long-term action effects and influence action selection.
Analyzes the learned planning algorithm and reports a strong resemblance to parallelized bidirectional search.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present their work as the first mechanistic evidence that model-free reinforcement learning agents can learn to plan.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that interventions on discovered plans in the agent’s representations show a causal effect on behavior.
The authors report that plan emergence coincides with the ability to benefit from additional test-time compute.
The authors report a strong resemblance between the learned planning algorithm and parallelized bidirectional search.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames whether model-free agents can learn to plan and presents the work as mechanistic evidence that they can.
Uses concept-based interpretability on the DRC model-free agent in Sokoban.
Probes concepts, examines plan formation, and intervenes on representations to test behavioral influence.
Links plan emergence with benefiting from additional test-time compute.
Characterizes the learned algorithm as resembling parallelized bidirectional search and connects the findings to emergent planning and reasoning in RL-trained LLMs.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a mechanistic claim with three analysis steps: concept probing, representation-level plan analysis, and behavioral interventions.

lessons.interpretation: This makes the proposed internal mechanism and its behavioral relevance explicit at separate levels of analysis.
lessons.application: When presenting an interpretability result, map each internal representation claim to a targeted probe and an intervention that tests whether it affects behavior.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when interventions are impossible, poorly controlled, or unrelated to the proposed mechanism.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify intervention design, controls, effect sizes, task scale, or the conditions under which additional test-time compute helps.
The reported resemblance to parallelized bidirectional search is qualitative; the abstract does not define the comparison criteria or establish algorithmic equivalence.
The abstract does not provide details sufficient to assess the scope of the claimed causal or mechanistic conclusions beyond DRC in Sokoban.
